p: Most software projects that go over budget do not fail because the developers cannot code. They fail because the people paying for the work and the people doing it had different pictures in their heads, and nobody wrote the picture down. A software requirements document, often shortened to SRS (software requirements specification), is that written picture.

This guide explains what belongs in a requirements document, how detailed it needs to be, and how to write one even if you have never worked with developers before. By the end you will have a structure you can copy, a worked example, and a checklist to run through before you ask anyone for a quote.

h: What a requirements document is, and what it is not
p: A requirements document describes what the software must do and the conditions it must meet. It does not describe how the code is organised, which database to use or what the buttons look like in pixels. Those are design and engineering decisions that your development team makes, ideally with your input.

Think of it as the brief you would give an architect. You would say how many people will live in the house, what the budget is, and that you need step-free access. You would not tell them where to put each brick. Keeping that line clear stops the document from becoming a 60-page burden that nobody reads, and it leaves room for the developers to suggest simpler solutions than the one you imagined.

It also is not a contract on its own, although it often becomes an attachment to one. Its main job is shared understanding. A good test of quality: someone who has never heard of your business should be able to read it and explain back what the software is for.

h: Start with the problem and the goal
p: Open the document with one short paragraph on the problem you are solving and one on how you will know it is solved. For example: staff spend two hours every morning copying orders from email into a spreadsheet, and errors cause wrong deliveries. The goal is that orders enter the system once and the delivery list is produced automatically.

This section matters more than it seems. When a developer later faces a decision the document does not cover, which always happens, they can ask which option better serves the goal. It also protects you from building features that sound impressive but do not move the needle.
Add a short list of constraints at this stage: the budget range, the launch date and why it matters, and anything fixed such as an existing accounting system that the new software must work with.

h: Describe the users and what each of them needs to do
p: List every type of person who will use the software, including those you might forget: administrators, customers, drivers, accountants, support staff. For each, write one or two lines about who they are and how comfortable they are with technology.

Then describe what each user needs to achieve, using the simple user-story format: as a type of user, I want to do something, so that I get some benefit. The benefit clause is the part people skip, and it is the most useful part because it explains the reason behind the request.
list: As a dispatcher, I want to see all unassigned deliveries on one screen, so that I can assign them before 9am.
As a customer, I want to receive a message when my order is on its way, so that I do not have to phone the shop.
As an owner, I want a weekly sales summary by product, so that I can decide what to reorder.

h: Functional requirements: what the system must do
p: Functional requirements are the specific behaviours the software must have. Group them by area, such as accounts and login, orders, payments, notifications and reporting, and number them so people can refer to them in conversation (for example, ORD-3).

Write each requirement as a short, single statement that can be checked. Compare two versions of the same idea. The vague version: the system should handle refunds. The clear version: a manager can refund all or part of a paid order; the customer is emailed a confirmation; the refund appears in the daily report. The second can be built, tested and priced. The first will be interpreted differently by everyone who reads it.

Mark each requirement as must have, should have or nice to have. Developers can then plan the first release around the must-haves and give you honest estimates for the rest. If everything is labelled must have, the labels have stopped doing their job.

These describe how well the system must work rather than what it does. They are the most commonly missing part of a requirements document and the source of many unpleasant surprises late in a project. Ask yourself each question below and write down the answer, even if the answer is that you do not mind.
list: Performance: how many people will use it at once, and how fast should the main pages and searches respond?
Security: who can see or change what? Does it handle payments, health details or other sensitive personal data?
Availability: can it be offline for maintenance, and when? What happens if it goes down during opening hours?
Devices: which phones, browsers and screen sizes must it support?
Accessibility: must it work with screen readers and keyboard-only use?
Data: how long must records be kept, and how are backups and deletion requests handled?
Compliance: are there industry or local rules, such as tax invoice formats or privacy laws, that apply?

p: Most business software does not live alone. List every other system it must exchange information with: payment providers, accounting packages, email or SMS services, maps, existing databases. For each, state the direction of the data (in, out or both), how often it moves, and who owns the account.

If you are replacing a spreadsheet or an old system, describe the existing data: roughly how many records, how clean they are, and which fields must be carried over. Data migration is routinely underestimated because it is invisible until the day it is attempted.

Finally, list the reports and exports you need. Ask the people who will read them what decisions the report supports. A report nobody can explain a use for is usually not worth building in the first release.

h: Say what is out of scope
p: A short out-of-scope list is one of the most valuable parts of the document. It records things you considered and deliberately postponed, such as a mobile app, multi-language support or a customer loyalty scheme. Writing them down prevents the quiet assumption that they were included and the awkward conversation when the invoice arrives.

It also makes later change requests easier. When a new idea appears mid-project, you can check it against the document, agree what it replaces or what it adds to the budget, and decide with open eyes.

h: A worked example: a booking tool for a small clinic
p: Imagine a small physiotherapy clinic with three therapists that currently takes bookings by phone and keeps a paper diary. The problem statement: reception spends a large part of the day on the phone, double bookings happen, and patients forget appointments. The goal: patients book and reschedule online, and reminders reduce no-shows.

Users: patients, therapists and the receptionist. Some patients are elderly and not comfortable with technology, so a phone option must remain. Must-haves: online booking against each therapist's availability, email and text reminders, a daily schedule view for each therapist, and a way for reception to override or edit any booking. Should-haves: online payment and a waiting list. Out of scope for version one: insurance claims, patient clinical notes and a mobile app.

Non-functional notes: patient details are personal data, so access must be limited by role and logged; the site must work on phones and with screen readers; and bookings must be backed up daily. Integrations: an SMS provider for reminders and the clinic's existing calendar. This is a single page of bullet points, and it is enough for two developers to give comparable, meaningful quotes.

h: Make requirements testable with acceptance criteria
p: For each important requirement, add acceptance criteria: the conditions that must be true for you to say it is finished. A simple format is given, when, then. Given a therapist is fully booked on Tuesday, when a patient searches for Tuesday, then no Tuesday slots are shown for that therapist.

Acceptance criteria turn opinions into checks. At delivery time you work through them together, rather than debating whether something feels right. They also help developers write automated tests, which protect the software from breaking when it is changed later.

list: Writing solutions instead of needs, such as demanding a specific button layout without saying what the user is trying to do.
Using vague words like fast, easy, flexible or modern. Replace them with something measurable or an example.
Leaving out the people who actually do the work. Speak to the receptionist, the driver or the accountant, not only the owner.
Treating the document as finished. It should be versioned and updated as decisions are made, with changes recorded.
Hiding uncertainty. If you do not know something, write it as an open question with an owner and a date, rather than guessing.

h: A step-by-step checklist before you ask for quotes
list: Write the problem, the goal and the constraints in one page.
List users and write user stories with a benefit for each.
Group and number functional requirements, and label priority.
Answer every non-functional question, even briefly.
List integrations, existing data and required reports.
Write an out-of-scope list and a list of open questions.
Add acceptance criteria to the ten most important requirements.
Ask someone outside the project to read it and explain it back to you.

p: How long should a requirements document be? As short as possible while still being unambiguous. A simple internal tool may need three to five pages, while a larger platform may need considerably more. Length is not a measure of quality; clarity is.

Do I need one if I use an agile approach? Yes, in a lighter form. Agile teams usually keep a prioritised backlog of user stories, which is a living requirements document. You still need the problem statement, constraints and non-functional needs up front.

Can I write it myself or do I need a business analyst? You can write a useful first draft yourself using the structure above. A developer or analyst can then review it, ask questions and fill gaps, which is much cheaper than starting from a blank page together.

What if my requirements change halfway through? They will, and that is normal. Record the change, assess its effect on time and cost, and update the document. The point is not to freeze decisions forever but to make changes visible and deliberate.

list: A requirements document records shared understanding: what the software must do, for whom and why.
Describe needs and outcomes, not screens and code, and write requirements that can be checked.
Do not forget non-functional needs such as security, performance, accessibility and data retention.
State what is out of scope and keep a list of open questions.
A clear one-to-five page document leads to better quotes, fewer surprises and a smoother project.
